accuracy.evidence: Matches Key Stage 3 science in England (diffusion in liquids and gases driven by differences in concentration; Brownian motion; the particle model). The ammonia and hydrogen chloride ring forms nearer the HCl end because NH3 (Mr 17) is lighter than HCl (Mr 36.5). The hot-vs-cold race uses water viscosity from 5 to 80 °C, so hot water really wins by several times; the lab says speeds are sped up.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the known errors: particles aim for the empty space (locked prediction on one particle, turn-back counter, challenge 'aim'), a draught is needed (lift step with no push, challenge 'fan', m4), particles stop at equilibrium (locked prediction, balanced crossing counter, m1, m8), low to high (p1, 'rev'), diffusion confused with a change of state (m6, 'evap') and liquid particles not moving ('still').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagdiff is a random-walk simulation with a removable divider, a live five-strip concentration bar chart, a traced path of one chosen particle with a turn-back count, a two-way crossing counter over the last 5 s, and two-box races with settable water temperatures and gas against liquid. No flag lab has a concentration gradient or crossing counts; the 6-token shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Pupils see each idea happen: purple spreads with no push, the traced particle turns back left again and again, the crossing counter shows more going right only while the left is crowded and then roughly equal numbers each way at equilibrium, and races show hot water and gases winning. The reason is in the picture, not a sentence.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions: whether one particle heads straight for the empty side, whether particles stop when the spread is even, which water temperature spreads ink faster (cold, hot or same), and gas vs liquid. Each is then tested directly in the simulation that follows.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions with tagged wrong answers: fan and aim (why perfume spreads), stop and side (equilibrium), cold and same (temperature), nh3 and mid (ammonia ring), rev and evap (definition), still and big (gas vs liquid). Each message names the mistake and gives the particle reason.

readability.evidence: Learner audience: kid text within the 6.5 limit and adult text within 9.5 as measured by the validator. Exact Key Stage 3 terms are used and defined: particle, random motion, collision, concentration, concentration gradient, net movement, equilibrium and diffusion.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean and overlap under 12 percent. Each kid paragraph adds one idea (definition with the perfume case, random motion and why the net flow happens, equilibrium, the two speed factors); adult paragraphs give curriculum, terms, named mistakes, the classic ammonia test and what each lab step shows.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 screenshots in both themes for every step: the single box fills the width with the bar chart and crossing counter under it, the two race boxes sit side by side with labels and percentages readable, and control buttons wrap in rows. walk.cjs passes on desktop and iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: axe finds no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark. Every canvas action has a button: lift the divider, follow a particle, fast-forward with aria-pressed, temperature up and down for each box, start the race and reset. The canvas aria-label and live text announce each result, and the tracked particle is shown by size and an amber trail, not colour alone.
